preamble: Devoicing of the voiced palatal stop /ɟ/ to /c/. In Khmer it was part of the general loss of voiced stops during the Middle Khmer period (completed between the late 16th and 18th centuries). The lost voicing survives as a vowel-register contrast: vowels after formerly voiced stops were first breathy, then took on different qualities. In West Slavic it happens synchronically through final devoicing, where /ɟ/ ď is pronounced [c] at the end of a word.

examples.to: Modern Khmer [cɛː] (high register, i.e. the formerly voiced series)
examples.note: Old Khmer /ɟ/ merged with /c/. The original voicing contrast is kept in the vowel: [ɟɛː] > [ɟɛ̤ː] > [cɛː], while original [cɛː] diphthongized to [caɛ].
Word-final obstruent devoicing turns ď /ɟ/ into [c]. Czech does the same, since its ď is also /ɟ/ and it devoices voiced obstruents before a pause.

sources: Wikipedia (2026). Middle Khmer: Devoicing of stops (after Jenner 1976; Headley 1998). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Khmer
